title: Pigeonhole Principle
description: A deceptively simple counting idea that proves surprising guarantees

blocks.text: The pigeonhole principle is one of the simplest ideas in mathematics, yet it proves surprisingly powerful results. It often turns a hard sounding problem into an obvious one.
The whole principle fits in a sentence, but recognising when to apply it is a genuine skill worth practicing.
If you put more items into fewer boxes, then at least one box must contain more than one item. Put 3 pigeons into 2 holes, and some hole holds at least 2 pigeons.

blocks.caption: With more pigeons than holes, at least one hole must contain two

blocks.text: Formally, if n items go into m boxes and n is greater than m, then some box has at least two items. That is the entire idea.

The principle feels almost too obvious to be useful, but its power is that it guarantees something must exist without telling you where. That kind of existence guarantee is exactly what many proofs and problems need.
The art is in choosing what the pigeons are and what the holes are. Once you pick the right mapping, the conclusion often falls out immediately.
There is a stronger version. If n items go into m boxes, then some box contains at least the ceiling of n divided by m items.

blocks.caption: The generalized principle guarantees a box with at least ceil(n / m) items

blocks.text: So 10 items in 3 boxes force some box to hold at least 4, since the ceiling of 10 over 3 is 4. This lets you prove not just that a collision happens, but how crowded it must get.
These well known results are all pigeonhole in disguise.

items: Among any 13 people, at least two share a birth month, since there are only 12 months.
In a drawer of 2 sock colours, picking 3 socks guarantees a matching pair.
Among any n plus 1 numbers chosen from 1 to n, two must be equal.
Among any n plus 1 integers, two leave the same remainder when divided by n.

blocks.text: That last one is a favourite in coding problems, because equal remainders mean their difference is divisible by n.
Here the remainders are the holes and the numbers are the pigeons. With more numbers than possible remainders, a repeat is guaranteed, and we can find it in one pass.
When a problem promises that something must exist among enough items, ask what the boxes are. The pigeonhole principle is often the hidden key.
